80.t: Calhoun classmates, the clarinet, and the dormitory combo
80.s: No one else from the band turned professional; his teacher told him to stay with the trumpet; he played in a dormitory combo but no dances.
80.ch: Boyhood in Evergreen and Calhoun school
80.q: Aw, I don't think so. I don't think so. No, not of the Calhoun band, no. No. There was a clarinetist there, Jack -- not Jack Butler. Hmmm.

80.t: Music background at Calhoun; the instruments owned by McDowell
80.s: His cousin's husband, a Hampton-trained clarinetist, made music strong there; he left his borrowed Evergreen horn, owned by the baseball-team owner who owned all the instruments.
80.ch: Boyhood in Evergreen and Calhoun school
80.q: Well, I got quite a bit because my cousin, she married the professor of Hampton Institute when he came there. He was quite a musician. He was -- had been in the First World War and playing clarinet, and he got his musical education from Hampden.

87.t: St. Emma's School in Virginia and its band
87.s: At 14 he went to a school near Richmond that had a band, where he began playing trombone.
87.ch: Virginia school and first Washington bands
87.q: Yeah, I went to school in Virginia about 40 miles out of -- I had been fooling around with a trombone a little bit around Savannah then. I went to this school

87.t: Band instruction at school under John Scott
87.s: They played marches and overtures, jazzed things up, and were taught by John Scott, a clarinetist.
87.ch: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
87.q: You play marches (unintelligible). We used to jazz up the marches sometime. They'd get after us and tell us to tone it down. We'd try to put some jazz notes in the marches. But we'd play a few overtures, things like the William Tell Overture, a few things. But mostly it was march. It was march…

453.t: The Biddle marching band under T. B. Jones
453.s: At Biddle he played in a 25-30 piece marching band; his improvised turn-back lines annoyed director T. B. Jones.
453.ch: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
453.q: yeah, I continued to study. I was in the band there, in the band there in Biddle. A fellow by the name of T. B. Jones had charge of the band. Yes.

453.t: Playing Coleridge-Taylor's Hiawatha's Wedding Feast at Biddle
453.s: First-chair trumpet on Coleridge-Taylor's piece with a violinist and a tenor soloist; he also notes the school became Johnson C. Smith.
453.ch: Biddle, Durham and early road shows
453.q: And, this is where I got a chance to really hear some good music. Did you ever hear of Coleridge S. Taylor? This was a colored composer. He composed "Hiawatha's Wedding Feast" -- one of the prettiest things you want to hear. I (unintelligible) first time I'd ever heard anything like that and I…

317.t: Jimmy's baritone horn, trombone and school music programs
317.s: Jimmy started on baritone horn, then trombone, and sang in an all-city choir; both praise school music being required in their cities.
317.q: Actually baritone horn was my first instrument, in terms of performing on it, because my arm wasn’t long enough to reach all the way out to the seventh position on the trombone, slide trombone you know. So the music instructor kind of smiled and says, “Look, see, you know you’ve got to grow a…

319.t: Trumpet, baritone horn and tuba in school
319.s: Under teacher Al Benest he starts trumpet in fourth grade, is moved to baritone horn, and is later offered tuba at the University of Washington.
319.q: Well it’s funny. I was a brass player all the time I was a kid. I wanted to be, my mother started me on piano and I hit a wall about the John M. Williams second book I think. I couldn’t get both hands to pay attention to what they were doing. But in the fourth grade a wonderful man came to our…

993.t: Starting on trombone, Henry Street Settlement and Howard Saposnik's junior high band
993.s: Band class, scholarship at Henry Street Settlement, and the band director who moved him to tuba.
993.q: My evolution into the tuba is that when I was very young, in elementary school they started a band program in my elementary school. And I brought the notice home to my mother and she was very excited. And so she signed me up for it, and I started, you know, so in those days you started as a class.…

606.t: Mellophone, North Texas State and switching to bass
606.s: He took up mellophone in high school, then bass at North Texas State, while always playing guitar.
606.ch: Schooling and the Soft Winds Trio
606.q: Gosh. I wanted to major in music. That’s why I went. And so the last year of high school I got a mellophone, you know a French horn? And I learned to play it and I learned to read a little bit see? So then I could get into football games. And then I went to North Texas State and I thought I’d take…

563.t: Youth bands and the International Youth Symphony
563.s: He played up through school, college and youth orchestras, and in seventh grade learned orchestral transposition in the International Youth Symphony.
563.q: Yeah, I started pretty quick. I mean early on I really took to playing the trumpet right away. I loved it and I just was one of those kids that my parents had to tell me to stop practicing, instead of trying to force me to practice. And so I progressed pretty rapidly. I practiced a lot and I played…

755.t: Growing up in Philadelphia playing brass
755.s: Midway through college in 1966, Kirsh recalls playing trombone and baritone horn and the strong Philadelphia school music program. A short aside about computer fan hiss follows.
755.ch: Music beginnings and entering the studio
755.q: I don’t know. I don’t know what the average listener is listening to, but I mean my interest was not listening for anything in particular, it was just enjoying the music. I started out as a musician playing, you know, through I guess grade school, junior high school, started playing brass…

162.t: Lessons with Professor Chambroka and the Rome White Band
162.s: His father took him to Chambroka, a firm clarinet-trained teacher; he also had a first school band at Thomas Street School.
162.q: No, my father brought me to Professor Chambroka who was with the Rome White Band Hall which is opposite Second Street if you know Rome. It’s still there, the hall where I took my first lesson. Prof Chambroka was a graduate of Milan Conservatory in Italy, and was an excellent teacher, but he just…

215.t: Goodman as a boyhood hero and the high school violins
215.s: Playing with Goodman was a thrill; his school orchestra's violins prepared him for Monroe's string section.
215.ch: New York studio and TV work
215.q: Oh that’s a big thrill too. I always think of that. And I always also think when I was in high school on our own time we had an orchestra. And I played the bass in the orchestra, because they had no guitar parts, but if they needed a guitar I could play it. But we had violins, we might have had 14…

823.t: Grammar school band and writing the Niantic School March
823.s: He describes the odd school band, the march he wrote in seventh grade and how the teacher transcribed it.
823.q: It was okay. I remember in grammar school there was a little old, Earl Barry, he was a violin player actually. A nice little old man with a moustache and we had a silly little band made up of around 19 violins, 4 or 5 mandolins, 3 or 4 or 5 maybe accordions, a bunch of metal clarinets, and a…

824.t: Willcox's boyhood, Manlius Military School and early bands
824.s: Willcox, born in Sherburne in 1903, learns his father's valve trombone, plays in the Manlius brass band, then Syracuse and Cornell bands, Whiteman's Collegians, the California Ramblers and Goldkette.
824.q: Yeah. You know when we drove into Norwich today, I saw a sign that said “Sherburne 12 miles” and remember I told you that that is where I was born, in Sherburne, New York in 1903, and moved to Cortland, New York in 1911 at eight years old. And so actually I was learning to play my father’s…

740.t: High school band and Mr. Klinger
740.s: He majored in art but spent time in the band room; Mr. Klinger got him into the band and gave him a chance to demonstrate percussion.
740.q: Sure. It makes a difference, a big difference. Someone to give you that push, you know? Say hey, why don’t you do that, and just press you on to it.

494.t: School music, sousaphone, bass lessons and schools attended
494.s: Theory in school, tuba in the marching band, bass lessons with a Philadelphia Orchestra player, and the schools he attended.
494.ch: Philadelphia roots and arrival in New York
494.q: Right, metal. I used to carry it home on the bus, people laughing at you. Bass, I started playing – I guess I was in high school. I don’t know what drew me to the bass. I know I liked it. I started studying with a – it was a bass player from the Philadelphia Orchestra. His name was George [?Inni],…

108.t: The Mastbaum School's classical music program
108.s: Strictly classical training in the symphonic band, with future professionals as classmates and Wilder in the third solo cornet chair.
108.ch: Childhood and learning music in Philadelphia
108.q: Oh yeah. When I was in junior high school, we used to play orchestral things. Then when I went to the Mastbaum School . . . .

509.t: Dunbar High School band, the cello that failed and the viola
509.s: At Dunbar she wanted cello but could not play it in a skirt, so played viola for about two years.
509.q: Yeah, I did. I was with the band and Mr. Grant. Mr. Grant was a wonderful man, and I wanted . . . well, anyway, I wanted to play cello, and my mother came one day and I‘m on the stage with the band. See, at that time you don‘t have pants. You know, you had a skirt, right.

67.t: What N. C. Davis taught: marches, no jazz
67.s: Davis was a military man teaching marches and church music, and jazz in rehearsal got the children scolded; school bands also banned it.
67.q: Well, the thing about it -- N. C. Davis was a military man, and he knew how to teach kids, and most of the things we were doing were marches, and we had a

380.t: Bordentown School, teacher Alexander Valentine, and meeting W.C. Handy
380.s: He enrolled at Bordentown School to join its travelling band, studied under Alexander Valentine, and was turned away by W.C. Handy when seeking work as a copyist.
380.q: So Bordentown School up in Bordentown, New Jersey, which was about 19 miles from Trenton, had a band that used to travel all over the state, they came to our school, and after hearing this band I just had to go. Fortunately, my parents were able to send me to this school. And that was my beginning…

70.t: Claude Jones at Wilberforce and the start of the septet
70.s: Claude Jones started on trombone at Wilberforce and joined the Synco Cinco Septet that became the Cotton Pickers.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: And McKinney had this band and for some reason or other in that orchestra they had a trombone. And McKinney didn't have no trombones, so Lawrence -- I mean, Claude -- gee whiz -- Claude Jones started fooling with the trombone while he was in school down there. And he got to playing with the Synco…

168.t: School orchestra repertoire and his proud parents
168.s: They played Sousa-type marches pizzicato without amplification; his parents came to hear him and were very proud.
168.ch: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
168.q: No, I don't remember. We probably had a couple of times when we played for maybe where the parents came in for assembly or a play of some sort, you know, school play, but that was -- I can't quite remember.

115.t: Perfect pitch and classmate Henry Coker
115.s: Gus has near-perfect pitch; Henry Coker, with his father's beat-up trombone, was in his music class.
115.q: Yeah, I was working in the drugstore and all like that, and riding the bicycle out. I started growing like that.

428.t: Masbaum vocational school: cello, tuba and music all day
428.s: He explains how he came to the tuba at Masbaum, the school's setup and graduates, and why he never played tuba in jazz.
428.ch: Philadelphia bands and the Club Harlem
428.q: The tuba came in when I went to Masbaum after Overbrook. And Masbaum was a school, Jules Masbaum was a philanthropist in Philadelphia who also promoted jazz music, like the Curtis family. That's why they named the school after him. And it was a vocational school but it was the first vocational…

7.t: Carpentry, Kansas Vocational Institute and band teacher William L. Dawson
7.s: Intending architecture, Thomas studies carpentry at the Tuskegee-style Kansas Vocational Institute, whose first band teacher, William L. Dawson, has a beautiful trombone tone.
7.q: Right. Now, guess who my first band teacher was! Man, how I got involved in music... My father wanted me to be an architect. So I went to school, and they had carpentry there, and I figured mechanical drawing, and carpentry was the nearest thing to me getting into architecture, because an architect…

171.t: Warm-Up Ramey and taking the tuba job from a football coach
171.s: He starred in basketball but warmed the football bench, apparently because he took the coach's tuba job in the Royal Aces.
171.ch: Growing up with music in Austin
171.q: right on going. But then we got it to working down, pretty good. And I began -- now my teacher -- now, I played football and basketball. I was like a star on the basketball team.

103.t: Edgar Battle and the Jack Hoxie show; study with James H. Wilson in Huntsville
103.s: Jones praises Edgar Battle as bandleader of Jack Hoxie's show, then describes studying at A and M in Huntsville with cornetist James H. Wilson.
103.q: of the band, but nobody had ever led. Jack Hoxey was a terrific cowboy like the Tom Mix here. But he had the One-O-One Ranch and who was the head bandmaster was Edgar Battle, a black man, not a white man. This was something that the Jet, Ebony, and the Pittsburgh Courier and nobody ever wrote…

98.t: School bands in Milwaukee and Tilden Tech, Sousa and Orchestra Hall
98.s: Details of the 18-20 piece Milwaukee brass band, then the Tilden Tech band where Sousa guest-conducted, and trips to hear Frederick Stock at Orchestra Hall.
98.ch: Childhood, first drums and the hustling years
98.q: Right, right, I was playing snare drum. Then we had a bass drummer, you know, and -- in the band, and I guess we had about 20 pieces, 18 or 20 pieces. It was a small brass band.

13.t: Wendell Phillips High School and learning tuba from Charlie Allen
13.s: Wilson enters Wendell Phillips, joins the ROTC band and is handed a beat-up tuba by Charlie Allen, who teaches him the fingering.
13.q: When I started in Phillips High School, a friend of mine belonged to the ROTC band, and I wanted to get in the band. So his name was Charlie Allen.
